function: Legitimate UAV MARL policies jointly set IoT transmit power, artificial-noise power, bandwidth, CPU shares, offloading ratio and trajectory to maximize worst-case IoT energy efficiency (p. 6-7).
system: 3 legitimate UAVs with two antennas, 3 eavesdropping UAVs, 20 IoT devices; Rician links, 6 MHz bandwidth, carrier not stated; no RIS (p. 3, 10).
method: Adversarial multi-agent reinforcement learning, ARL-MAPPO: MLP actor-critic, centralized training, distributed execution; legitimate and eavesdropping UAVs trained alternately with a set of past adversary policies (p. 8-10).
data_channel: Custom Python simulator: Rician fading (10 dB), path-loss factor 2.2, 1000 m square area, random IoT positions; no standardized or measured channel (p. 4, 10).
test_conditions: Training: legitimate UAVs against alternating eavesdropper policies; evaluation: fixed legitimate policy against newly trained eavesdroppers; 1-5 eavesdroppers or 1-5 legitimate UAVs per scenario (p. 11-13).
baselines: Four MAPPO-based baselines differing only in the eavesdropper policy used in training: fixed, random, circular trajectory, and MAPPO-agent eavesdroppers (p. 10); no non-learned baseline.
metrics: Worst-case energy efficiency of IoT devices (weighted success and delay over energy), execution delay, execution success rate, IoT energy consumption (p. 6, 11-12).
complexity: none; only a qualitative remark of slower convergence and higher training cost (p. 12).
q1_support: p. 4: "be modeled by the Rician fading channel"; Table I (p. 10) gives Rician factor 10 dB and path loss factor 2.2. Custom simulator; no 3GPP model, COST 2100, DeepMIMO or measured data is mentioned.
q2_support: p. 11: "the phase in which the eavesdropping UAVs are used as agents of MAPPO (the blue curved part of Fig. 3) is essentially the same as the evaluation phase"; p. 12: "when training and evaluation with different numbers of eavesdropping UAVs". No model trained in one configuration is tested in another.
q3_support: p. 10: "All four baseline schemes are based on the MAPPO algorithm for policy optimization of legitimate UAVs, differing only in the policy of the eavesdropping UAVs selected for training." No non-learned method is compared for the legitimate-UAV policy; Baselines 1-3 are the proposed method trained against fixed, random or circular eavesdroppers.
q4_support: p. 12: "has slower convergence and higher training costs though", a qualitative statement only. No order of complexity, FLOPs, parameter count or runtime is reported; p. 10 gives only the MLP sizes (three hidden layers, 64 and 128 nodes).
q5_support: p. 10: "The programming language used in the experiments is Python and the deep learning framework used is Pytorch". No code or data link and no public channel dataset; the channel comes from a custom simulator (p. 4).
notes: Included as area 6. The learned UAV policies control IoT transmit power, artificial-noise power and spectrum (bandwidth) allocation on UAV links, which is physical layer in aerial links, jointly with offloading ratio, CPU shares and trajectory, which are above it (p. 6: "which include trajectory, spectrum resource, and computational resource allocation, as well as the transmission power of IoT devices"; action vector in Eq. 24, p. 7), so the above_phy check passes by the joint rule. Physical-layer security with artificial noise, not anti-jamming. The reviewer should confirm that this UAV-enabled MEC work counts as area 6. q2 is 0 because for the proposed method the evaluation stage is the last training phase (p. 11) and the scenarios with 1-5 UAVs are trained and evaluated each (p. 12); for the baselines the evaluation eavesdropper differs from training, but that is not the proposed model. Tables I and II were read from the PDF image of pp. 10 and 12, since they were not in the extracted text.
